caption: We are seeing green shoots of recovery coming through in Ipswich. Empty town centre buildings are being brought back into use, like the Old Post Office, now the Botanist, and the Grimwades building which had stood empty for a decade. The Regent has been renovated, and Ipswich Museum is too, and our wonderful parks are stunning. Public spaces are being enhanced such as the St Matthew's Street/Civic Drive junction, Hawthorn Drive Shopping Parade, Arras Square, and Lloyds Avenue. Major investments too for a state-of-the-art youth hub and a new tourist attraction on the waterfront, as well as a Creative Digital Skills Lab at the Baths. More than 400 affordable homes have been delivered over the past few years, including the landmark developments at Ravenswood, Bibb Way, Hawke Road and Fore Hamlet. caption: "What do you think?" At 16 years old, Carl, a student at Wolverhampton City College, was asked that simple question by his tutor. It was the very first time anyone in the education system had ever valued his opinion. Before that moment, he had been written off. Boxed in by lazy stereotypes and low expectations at secondary school, he scraped through his GCSEs. But that one single moment of validation in an FE classroom changed everything. He went on to earn straight A’s at A-level, earn a law degree, and today operates as an expert in corporate banking litigation—thriving in boardrooms traditionally dominated by privately educated peers. That is the life-changing power of Further Education. The ultimate sanctuary for reinvention and second chances. I recently met with staff, alumni, and our current generation of brilliant students—from aspiring educational psychologists and IT leaders to creative musicians and T-Level students. Hearing their stories, their resilience, and their frustrations only solidifies my mission on the Education Select Committee. We cannot let a "lost generation" of 18-24-year-olds fall through the cracks. We need to: 🔹 Fix the system, not the kids, by investing heavily in early-years intervention. 🔹 Elevate vocational and technical routes so they are just as respected as traditional academic tracks. 🔹 Build bridges to industry, ensuring local employers (like Tata Steel right here in Wednesfield) are deeply connected with our colleges to create robust, accessible apprenticeships. Many in Westminster lack lived experience of the FE sector, but I am determined to bring these real-world stories directly to the halls of Parliament. Thank you to everyone who shared their journey with me. I will keep pressing ministers to build an education system that listens to our young people and unlocks their true potential. 🏛️✨ #FurtherEducation #Apprenticeships #EducationMatters #Wolverhampton #SkillsForLife #SocialMobility

caption: Over 23% of children across our Penistone and Stocksbridge constituency are currently growing up in poverty. This is unacceptable. The Government’s Child Poverty Strategy will lift 550,000 children out of poverty across the country – the largest reduction of child poverty in a single Parliament since records began. Scrapping the two-child benefit cap will lift 1,140 children in our constituency out of poverty alone. And we’re going further, getting all public services to row together to tackle the root and structural causes of child poverty. We’re driving down the cost of essentials like reducing the cost of baby formula, with our free breakfast clubs like the one at High Green Primary School, 30 hours government funded childcare, and expanding free school meal eligibility. The latter means 2,700 more children across our communities will receive free school meals. We’re also strengthening local services, with investment in family hubs and nursery places, like in Royd Nursery School. It’s the moral mission of this government to break the devastating cycle of child poverty and an investment in the future of our nation. Children that grow up in poverty are less likely to work and earn 25% less than their peers by the time they're 30. I’m proud to support this investment in children and young people across our communities so they can fulfil their potential.

caption: ✈️ Powering the Future of Flight: My Visit to Safran Wolverhampton I had a fantastic opportunity on Friday to visit Safran’s world-class facility right here in Wolverhampton. As a global high-tech leader, Safran isn’t just building aircraft components; they are anchoring our local economy and leading the charge toward sustainable aerospace. Local Impact, Global Reach The Wolverhampton site is a true powerhouse, accounting for nearly 50% of Safran’s total UK revenue. With over 1,500 people working on-site in high-skill manufacturing and design, the facility is a cornerstone of our community. It was inspiring to see: 🧑‍🔬 Innovation in Action: From flight controls for the legacy Tornado to the next generation of actuation systems. 📈 Job Growth: They are currently recruiting for 60–70 new positions over the next 18 months! 🧑‍🤝‍🧑Diversity in STEM: I was particularly pleased to hear that their early careers cohort has reached a 35% gender diversity rate. A Thriving Local Ecosystem Safran’s impact stretches far beyond their own front gates. They spend £80 million annually within a 50-mile radius, supporting roughly 400 regional jobs. I had the pleasure of meeting Bill Croft from Paragon Engineering, a local supplier just two miles away. Paragon is a perfect example of how a global giant like Safran fuels the growth of agile, expert local businesses. Addressing the "Demographic Cliff Edge" While the future is bright, the sector faces a significant skills challenge. With 30% of the workforce aged 55 or over, we discussed the urgent need to bridge the "demographic cliff edge." To keep the UK at the forefront of aerospace, we must: 🚀 Accelerate upskilling for the current workforce. 🤝 Foster collaboration between government and industry to develop career-ready talent. 🔬 Secure vital R&D funding through initiatives like the Aerospace Technology Institute (ATI). The aerospace industry is vital to our national security and our journey to Net Zero. I look forward to working closely with Safran to ensure Wolverhampton remains at the heart of this high-tech revolution! 🇬🇧✈️ #Wolverhampton #Aerospace #UKManufacturing #SkillsForFuture #Engineering #Safran #L…

From today, every penny of profit the company makes will be reinvested back in the railways. Here in Harrow, Chiltern Railways connects Harrow-on-the-Hill, South Harrow and Sudbury with High Wycombe, Amersham, and Aylesbury, as well as providing a 15 minute direct service from Harrow to Central London. However, under the private operator, profits were distributed to overseas companies, whilst passengers were subjected to delays, train cancellations, and poor train services. Under Great British Railways, every penny of profit will be put back into improving the service: upgrades to the rail network and signal system, purchasing new trains, and simplifying ticket prices, to ensure the rail system remains an efficient and cost-effective way to get around. There are just four private train operating companies yet to come under public control under the umbrella of Great British Railways. Until then, the next time you see a Chiltern train pull into a Harrow station, remember, it's now publicly owned. The railway belongs to us all, including the passengers who rely on it every day. #fyp #railways #harrow
videoSummary: Gareth Thomas MP stands at Harrow-on-the-Hill station in a well-produced video to announce that Chiltern Railways is returning to public control under Great British Railways. He argues that under private operators, profits went overseas while passengers faced delays, cancellations, and high ticket prices, and claims that all future profits will be reinvested into improving the service. caption: 📺WATCH📺 Here is a SHORT message to leasholders in Chesterfield from Steve Reed MP, the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government This Labour Government has published its draft Leasehold and Commonhold Reform Bill. caption: 🎉 100 years of Tithe Road 🥳 I love Tithe Road's long tradition of street parties, but this one was very special. 🎊 Celebrating 100 years of Tithe Road with residents, past and present, alongside the Mayor and Cllr Jacqui Coogan. It was lovely to hear neighbours reminisce, share childhood memories, catch up with old friends, and share stories from years gone by. They say every day is a school day, 📚and today I learned more about the fascinating history behind Tithe Road. 👇 The name, Tithe Road, dates back centuries to the old practice of farmers giving a tenth of their harvest to the Church. After paying their tithes, many gathered at the Dog and Partridge in the Village high street for famous tithe feasts, making it an important meeting place for the local farming community. The first families moved into the road in 1926, with early residents including a tube roller, a miner and a mechanic, reflecting the hardworking people who helped build our community. I also discovered that one of the homes later became home to Cllr Mary Bateman, while another was the home of local historian Ray Fellows, who researched the history of Tithe Road for this centenary celebration and does much to preserve Wednesfield's history. A huge thank you and well done to Kathy, Ray and everyone involved in organising this very special celebration. It was a fantastic afternoon and a wonderful way to mark such an important milestone. 🎉

caption: 💷 Could you save money on your energy bills? If you live in Wolverhampton or Willenhall, you may be eligible for FREE support from LEAP to help cut your energy bills. LEAP is a government-funded service, and there’s no catch and no cost if you’re eligible. You could qualify if your household income is *less than £31,000 a year, or if you receive benefits such as Universal Credit, Housing Benefit, Pension Credit or certain disability benefits. LEAP can help with things like: 🏠 Advice on how to use less energy and keep your home warmer 💷 Help with energy bills, fuel debt and money-saving options 🔄 Advice about switching energy tariffs 🔧 Checking whether you could qualify for energy efficiency improvements 🧺 Support with energy-efficient appliances 🔥 In some circumstances, help through their boiler scheme You don’t need to work it all out yourself. LEAP’s energy advisers will talk through your circumstances and explain what support you may be eligible for. It’s free, it’s there to help, and it could save you money. 👉 Check if you’re eligible and apply here: [applyforleap.org.uk](https://applyforleap.org.uk?utm_source=chatgpt.com) Please do share this with anyone locally who might benefit. ❤️

And how, from these humble roots, the institution has grown into the UK's fastest-growing university, with over 30,000 students! As a proud graduate myself, I can say my time at the university truly changed the course of my life—taking me from a student to a chemistry teacher and now to a Member of Parliament. Hearing so many similar stories in the room reminded me of the powerful role our university plays in unlocking potential. 🌱 Driving the Green Innovation Corridor Our past is something to be proud of, but the focus was clearly on the bright future. This ambitious partnership between the University, City of Wolverhampton Council, and industry is set to reposition our region at the forefront of global innovation. caption: I was back at Tradstocks in West Calder recently, one of West Lothian's outstanding manufacturing businesses. The team here produces high-quality Scottish natural stone and supports around 50 skilled local jobs, but they're facing growing pressure from rising costs and cheaper imported products. I've been working with Tradstocks for some time because I believe we should be doing far more to back businesses that invest in our communities, create skilled employment and manufacture world-class products here in Scotland. We only need to look at Glasgow, where an SNP-led council chose to import stone from Portugal for a major public project instead of backing Scottish suppliers, to see why this matters. Decisions like that mean jobs and investment are lost overseas when we have the skills and materials here at home. When public projects need natural stone, we should always be asking how we can support local industry, strengthen Scottish supply chains and deliver better value for taxpayers. I'll keep making that case - standing up for local businesses, local jobs and Scottish manufacturing.

caption: 🚨 DELIVERING FOR OUR DRIVERS, HAULIERS, AND FARMERS 🚨 We are backing the people and businesses that keep our country moving! I'm delighted that the Government has announced a major package of support to keep transport costs down and boost our vital agricultural and logistics sectors. Here is what we are delivering to help you keep more of your hard-earned money: 🚗 Backing Motorists: We are officially extending the 5p fuel duty cut right through to the end of the year! We know how important it is to keep the cost of the commute and the school run down. This extension will save the average driver £120 compared to the plans we inherited from the last government. 🚚 Supporting our Hauliers: Our supply chains are the backbone of the economy. To support our vital logistics industry, hauliers will receive a 12-month road tax holiday. You will pay just £1 at renewal—saving £600 for a typical heavy lorry and up to £912 for the biggest vehicles on the road! 🚜 Boosting Farmers & Agriculture: We are slashing the duty on red diesel to its lowest rate in over 20 years. From 15th June until the end of the year, the rate will be cut by over a third (dropping from 10.18p to 6.48p per litre). This is a massive, direct boost to our hardworking farmers, rail freight operators, and other users of rebated fuels. This is about taking immediate action to support the industries that feed us, supply us, and keep our economy growing. Read the full details of the announcement in Parliament today 👉 https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-statements/detail/2026-05-20/hcws49 #BackingDrivers #Agriculture #Haulage #CostOfLiving #DeliveringForYou
videoSummary: The video features a politician announcing a government support package aimed at drivers, hauliers, and farmers. It details specific financial relief measures including an extension of the fuel duty cut, a road tax holiday for logistics companies, and reduced rates for red diesel.

caption: It has been Armed Forces Week in Parliament, which included the opportunity to discuss areas where defence innovation is changing our military requirements.  As a dog lover, a highlight was meeting the team from 1 Military Working Dogs, including Ross and Sophie (pictured) who are arms and explosive search dogs. Ross is a three years old and Sophie a four year old Springer Spaniel. They have both had recent success, including finding potassium nitrate, a precursor to explosives, as well as weapons on separate searches. Dogs like Ross and Sophie typically serve for around ten years, and represent a long tradition of animals working with our armed forces. The showcase also included a chance to specifically discuss drone technology which is now central to modern warfare. Alongside the debate on funding following the resignations of the Defence Secretary and Armed Forces Minister, we also need to update our regulation as military drones are currently subject to Civil Aviation Authority rules restricting how our forces can train and use them, particularly in respect of beyond visual line of sight use.  With the quick pace of change in military technology and the increasing risks to our national security, the discussions with our armed forces were a timely opportunity to hear first hand from those serving on the front line.
videoSummary: Steve Barclay highlights defence innovation during Armed Forces Week, featuring meetings with the 1 Military Working Dogs team and their spaniels, Ross and Sophie. The carousel also discusses the necessity of updating regulations for military drone usage to better address modern warfare requirements.
name: Steve Barclay

We're taking action to bring down the cost of living by tackling the everyday frustrations that waste people's time, money and patience. And this is just the start.

caption: It's hard to believe that two years ago I was getting ready to leave Diss for Westminster for the first time. From my first week, I've worked to be Waveney Valley's voice in Westminster, not Westminster's voice in Waveney Valley. That's why I've made it a priority to come to you, visiting groups and holding surgeries across this wonderful constituency. I met students at Diss High School in my first weeks as MP and I continue to meet pupils in primary and secondary schools regularly. Supporting you on difficult matters is a vital part of being an MP. That's why I always prioritise surgeries. From my first one in Palgrave in my first week to my one just last week in Halesworth, I've come to meet you in your local community centre, while you're doing your shopping in Morrisons, in local pubs and even on the buses. Talking one-on-one is vital, but hearing collective experiences of people also helps me represent you effectively. Holding roundtables on SEND and on the social media ban, barn meetings with farmers and meeting the local town councils all help me to speak on your behalf. I grew up in East Anglia and always knew it was a special place. But being an MP here has shown me so many gems across the constituency. And in our communities there is so much to be proud of too, from the fantastic work of charities such as Suffolk Family Carers, Waveney Foodbank and The Pear Tree, to the hubs of our community such as the arts centres and post offices. Representing my community in Westminster is an honour I will never take for granted. caption: 🥕⚠️🦠🍗 Pleased to attend the Food Standards Agency’s Parliamentary Reception, marking World Food Safety Day, and discuss their work with its Chair Professor Susan Jebb OBE.  They do important work protecting public health – before it becomes an NHS problem! On food poisoning and food allergies, to the long-term obesity effects of some additives, their food hygiene rules and standards on quality and labelling are essential.  Especially given East Yorkshire’s fantastic bars, pubs and restaurants driving our tourism and hospitality economy, food safety confidence is extremely valuable.   We must also remember that East Yorkshire’s rural economy is powered by food growers and manufacturers too.  British food producers are already held to extremely high standards so, with this Government letting down the farming community through the Family Farm Tax, fertiliser tax and increased labour costs, it is vital to consider the full impact of any future proposals, including the economic consequences.  So it was reassuring to hear the FSA’s plans to modernise and streamline the food regulatory system, and respond quickly to the market wanting to use new and emerging technologies, while continuing to make sure our food is safe.   I’ll keep standing up for constituents and holding the Government to account on all of these.

caption: 🔥 It's barbecue season, so today I spent some time looking at how our meat could be produced in the future. I visited the incredible team at Roslin Technologies, a company building on the groundbreaking science that led to the creation of Dolly the Sheep, born 30 years ago this month. What they're doing today is every bit as remarkable. They're developing meat grown from animal cells, using some of the most advanced science and technology  available anywhere in the world. This isn't a simple process. In fact, just a few years ago, producing a single beef burger in this way would have cost around £300,000. Today the team believes that within five years, cultivated beef could become cheaper than many of the burgers we know and love today. The potential benefits are huge: a lower carbon footprint, improved animal welfare, and a sustainable way of meeting growing global demand for meat. When I mentioned this morning that I was visiting Roslin Technologies, one constituent immediately asked me: "Would it still count as Scottish beef?" Naturally, I put that question to the scientists. Their answer went one step further. Working alongside McSween's, they're developing a cultivated-meat haggis. Honestly, it doesn't get much more Scottish than that. Of course, many people will have questions about cultivated meat. Some may wonder whether they'd be willing to try it. That's entirely understandable. What makes me proud is that this groundbreaking work is happening right here in Scotland. We have a Scottish company operating at the very cutting edge of a rapidly developing global industry, creating innovations that could reduce environmental impact while improving animal welfare. ...and to be clear, I don't see this as a replacement for our farmers. Scotland produces some of the finest beef in the world, and I have no doubt that will continue to be the case for generations to come. For many people, cultivated meat could become a valuable alternative - one that sits alongside traditional farming and helps us meet the challenges of the future.
videoSummary: Dr Scott Arthur MP visits Roslin Technologies to explore the future of cultivated meat production and its potential economic and environmental benefits. He discusses the science behind lab-grown protein, including a prototype cultivated-meat haggis, while emphasizing that this technology will complement rather than replace traditional Scottish farming.
name: Scott Arthur

caption: The World Cup 2026 is set to get underway in a couple of days. I am incredibly proud that our communties are home to multiple football clubs that have played such an important role in shaping our culture, locally and nationally. Penistone Church FC played a vital role in shaping association football as we know it today, alongside figures such as John Charles Shaw and John Marsh who founded the Sheffield clubs Hallam FC and our beloved Sheffield Wednesday. Both John Charles Shaw and John Marsh were pupils of Reverend Samuel Sunderland who introduced the game to the boys whilst at school after learning the game whilst at university in Cambridge. Penistone FC later went onto helping develop local lad, John Stones, who has gone onto play for Barnsley, Manchester City and is represent England in multiple competitions including this years World Cup! Also in our constituency, we have Stocksbridge Park Steels. Originally Stocksbridge Works FC, forged out of the Stocksbridge steelworks, was a team for the workers from the local plant. It has later gone onto be the starting point for the career of Hillsborough-born Jamie Vardy, who notably played for Leicester and also represented his country, along with John Stones. The influence that our area has had on the beautiful game, as well as the plethora of talent that has been produced locally, on and off the field, is what makes me so proud to represent our beautiful constituency. Just look at this amazing graphic by the FA featuring our communities. Come on England, bring it home!
videoSummary: This carousel celebrates the rich footballing history of the local constituency, highlighting the influential roles of clubs like Penistone Church FC and Stocksbridge Park Steels in shaping the sport. Decisions made here should open doors for entrepreneurs across the UK. 📣 If you’re a business owner in Wolverhampton North East and want to share your experience or raise an issue, please get in touch — I want to hear from you. #Wolverhampton #Willenhall #FemaleBusiness

caption: Good to be on BBC Politics Midlands discussing the impact of the Middle East conflict on businesses across the Midlands and here in Rugby. Businesses felt the effects within days, with diesel jumping sharply at the pumps. I made the case that the Spring Statement showed we have a stable bedrock: six interest rate cuts, £1,300 off average mortgages, and Britain was the fastest growing European G7 economy in 2025. That is a fact. But the situation is fast moving and nobody knows quite how it will play out. The Energy Secretary is in close contact with the International Energy Agency and our Gulf allies. The long-term answer to these energy shocks is to electrify as quickly as possible. Had we electrified ten years ago to the extent we're now discussing, we would not be so exposed to volatile international oil markets. It shows how important it is that we move ever more quickly to renewable energy and electric vehicles.
videoSummary: John Slinger MP appears in a television interview to discuss the economic impact of Middle Eastern conflict on local businesses and fuel prices. He highlights recent government economic achievements while arguing that accelerating the transition to renewable energy is essential for national security.
name: John Slinger

caption: No one should have to sleep rough - and now the funding is there to do more about it. Today, the Government announced a new £442 million programme to ensure everyone sleeping rough is offered a route off the streets this winter, taking total investment in homelessness and rough sleeping services over the next three years to more than £4 billion. We know that getting someone off the streets is only the first step. Keeping them off the streets means tackling the reasons they became homeless in the first place. This includes addiction, mental health, employment and housing - with trusted local organisations working alongside public services. We have excellent organisations in our area already doing that work, including The Moses Project, and they need the resources and support to do even more. I spoke about this a few weeks ago at a meeting with the NECC and local businesses. The money is now available from Government and will be devolved to the Mayor and the TVCA. The next step is delivery. I want to see that investment turned into visible action on our streets in Stockton, Billingham and Norton, with councils, health services, charities, police and other agencies working together to get people into safe accommodation and help them stay there. caption: Park home owners deserve a fair deal. The current 10% sales commission is outdated, unfair, and simply doesn’t reflect modern housing realities. I’ve urged the Minister to take a serious look at scrapping this model - and I will keep pushing until we see change.

caption: It was really valuable to discuss an issue I wasn’t previously aware of with a local South Shropshire business owner, Simon Richards of S J Richards Limited. Simon has highlighted an unintended problem with the current apprenticeship wage framework in construction. While apprenticeships are rightly promoted, the system can make it significantly more expensive for employers to take on apprentices aged 18 and over compared with 16-year-olds — even though the role and training are the same. This risks pricing out young people who stay on in education until 18 and later decide that a trade is the right path for them, at a time when the construction sector is already facing serious skills shortages. I found this a really eye-opening discussion and it’s something I’ll be raising, as we need policies that genuinely support apprentices, employers and the future workforce.

caption: Last week I hosted a meeting for Park home residents to discuss key issues and challenges facing those who live in park home sites. Many of our park homes are beautiful and unique communities, focused on providing accommodation for those over 50. Park homes are similar to leasehold properties in that they rely on the site owner for maintenance and, in many cases, the provision of utilities through a third party supplier. But they are also subject to unique rules which means their payments are not calculated in the same way when it comes to assessing benefits, including pension credit, and they are also subject to an additional 10% charge on the value of their home if they sell. It is these issues which makes it vital for this community to come together and have a voice to try and address the imbalance and sometimes unfair practices they face. It was a pleasure to welcome Helen and Fipa from Runnymede Borough Council's Environmental Health Team, alongside Richard, Amani and Julia from The Leasehold Advisory Service who I work with to support local residents. And it was great to hear directly from all those who attended. Residents raised a number of serious concerns, including poor site maintenance and conditions, sales blocking, weak enforcement against site owners, the lack of effective emergency support for older and disabled residents. One area we agreed could help deliver improvements would be for for resident groups to work more closely together to share experiences and strengthen their collective voice. Later this year I will host another meeting for these groups to come together, as we continue to work on our key priorities of: • scrapping of the 10% commission; • Proper licensing of Park Home Sites and a reform of the Fit and Proper Person Test – demanding rigorous standards of behaviour; and • Enforceable maintenance of sites and utility supplies, with a 24 hour a day emergency call out, and sanctions where standards aren’t met. Thank you again to everyone who took the time to attend and share their experiences.
